main_goals.goal: Maintain and improve the Windows PyQt5 CDDA JSON mod editor

architecture.style: Small PyQt5 desktop application with gradually separated parsing/project/UI modules

layers.name: application package
layers.responsibility: Desktop application source code and package entry point.

layers.name: project model
layers.responsibility: Load mod JSON files, classify objects by schema, track dirty files, and create/delete mod objects.

layers.name: json io
layers.responsibility: Read and write CDDA-style JSON with comments and reference-mod compatibility.

layers.name: ui
layers.responsibility: PyQt5 windows, widgets, menus, theme handling, and object editing workflow.

layers.name: automated tests
layers.responsibility: unittest checks for parser behavior and Slaanesh reference mod loading.

layers.name: reference mod
layers.responsibility: Reference CDDA mod kept in the workspace for manual checks and file comparison after editor saves.

notes: This is a real Windows 10 PyQt5 application, not the reusable project-template skeleton.
Slaanesh is a reference mod and must not be deleted or treated as disposable build output.
build/ and dist/ may remain in the shared working folder because they are used for the ready build workflow, but generated files should not be tracked in Git.
Keep changes incremental and preserve the current script-style launch while adding package/Poetry support.
Automated tests should use the standard library where practical so the project remains easy to validate on Windows.

logging.policy: No dedicated logging adapter exists yet; keep parse/load warnings visible and avoid adding unrelated logging infrastructure during packaging work.

rules.rule: TDD is mandatory: every behavior change starts with tests (new/updated failing test first), then implementation.
For TDD work, explicitly run the new or updated tests in a failing state before changing implementation code; only after observing the failure may the code be changed to make the tests pass.
Priority principle: higher numeric priority means stricter precedence.
Clean Architecture is mandatory: keep boundaries between domain, application, infrastructure, and delivery layers.
Before any code changes, update status_worker.json with request analysis, planned scope, and validation plan.
Before starting any task, read status_worker.json to refresh project context, constraints, and last known validation state.
Run make check after changes that can affect behavior or quality gates.
If automated tests require fixture or sample files, store them under ./tests/files/<test_class>/<test_name> rather than scattering them across the repository.
Group tests into semantically meaningful test classes so test names stay concise and behavior remains easy to scan.
Test output must be verbose, and make command output must expose executed checks through explicit echo messages so the run shows steps, individual test cases, and a useful result summary.
Use ./vendor/loggerfactory for project logging and emit level-appropriate messages in infrastructure, application orchestration, and delivery code where operational visibility is needed.
After tests pass successfully, review the resulting code against the current project requirements and all rules recorded in status_worker.json before considering the task complete.
Documentation must match program behavior after interface/flow/rule changes.
Project documentation must be maintained in Russian unless a separate explicit requirement defines another language for a specific document.
When a task is completed, set its status to completed and reduce its priority to the minimum active planning priority so unfinished work remains visually and operationally ahead of completed items.
After completing a task, update status_worker.json to reflect the result and synchronize README.md with the current project state when relevant.
After completing a task, update project documentation in ./docs/ so the detailed technical documentation stays aligned with the implemented behavior and decisions.
If all currently tracked tasks are completed, summarize the result and then define or clarify the next backlog of tasks before considering planning finished.

practice_1.title: Red-Green-Refactor in small steps
practice_1.practice: Write a failing test first, implement only enough code to make it pass, then refactor while keeping the tests green.
practice_1.why: Small red-green-refactor cycles reduce risk, keep intent explicit, and prevent overbuilding beyond the currently specified behavior.

practice_2.title: Use tests to specify behavior, not incidental implementation
practice_2.practice: Create tests around externally visible behavior and decision rules instead of binding them tightly to internal implementation details.
practice_2.why: Behavior-focused tests remain stable during refactoring and better protect the intended business outcome.

practice_3.title: Maintain a self-testing codebase
practice_3.practice: Keep the project in a state where automated tests run frequently and failures immediately block confidence in the change.
practice_3.why: Fast automated feedback is the practical foundation that makes TDD useful instead of ceremonial.

practice_4.title: Refactor continuously under test protection
practice_4.practice: Once behavior is protected by tests, improve structure, naming, duplication, and design continuously instead of postponing refactoring.
practice_4.why: TDD is not complete at green status alone; design quality comes from the refactor step performed with test safety.

practice_1.title: Docs-as-code
practice_1.practice: Keep documentation in the same workflow as code: version control, code review, and automation should apply to docs alongside implementation changes.
practice_1.why: This keeps documentation current while features are fresh and prevents docs from drifting away from the codebase.

practice_2.title: Document before and during implementation
practice_2.practice: Start documenting requirements, assumptions, and intended behavior before coding, then refine that documentation during implementation instead of postponing it until the end.
practice_2.why: Early documentation clarifies scope, improves decisions, and gives the team a usable first draft before code details get lost.

practice_3.title: Test documentation continuously
practice_3.practice: Run documentation checks in continuous integration and on regular commits so docs build cleanly, examples stay valid, and documentation regressions are caught early.
practice_3.why: Documentation that is not tested degrades quickly, especially examples, commands, and generated outputs.

practice_4.title: Write for clarity, consistency, and explicit scope
practice_4.practice: Document the audience, scope, terminology, and structure explicitly; keep wording consistent so readers can quickly find the right meaning and action.
practice_4.why: Stable terminology and predictable structure reduce ambiguity and make technical documentation easier to scan and maintain.

practice_5.title: Review documentation for quality and accessibility
practice_5.practice: Treat documentation review like code review: perform peer editing, re-read drafts with fresh context, and verify that instructions and structure remain accessible and usable.
practice_5.why: A review pass catches missing context, wording issues, accessibility problems, and hidden assumptions that tests alone do not catch.

practice_1.title: Dependencies point inward
practice_1.practice: Outer layers may depend on inner layers, but domain and application rules must not depend on frameworks, UI, databases, or delivery details.
practice_1.why: This preserves business rules as the stable center of the system and keeps implementation details replaceable.

practice_2.title: Separate policies from details
practice_2.practice: Keep business decisions and use cases in core layers, while infrastructure, persistence, transport, and tooling remain adapters around them.
practice_2.why: This makes the system easier to test, evolve, and port without rewriting domain logic for each technical detail.

practice_3.title: Define interfaces at the boundary of the core
practice_3.practice: Express persistence and external integration needs as interfaces owned by the core or application layer, with concrete adapters implemented outside.
practice_3.why: Boundary interfaces allow the core to control collaboration contracts while keeping external technologies replaceable.

practice_4.title: Test the core without infrastructure
practice_4.practice: Design domain and application code so core use cases can be tested without real databases, web layers, or framework bootstrapping.
practice_4.why: If the core needs infrastructure to be tested, the architecture boundaries are already too weak.
